metric_rationale: The experimental design pits Take The Best (TTB) against Tallying. In almost all trials, the option favored by the single most valid discriminating cue (TTB's choice) is opposed by the option that wins on a larger number of less valid cues (Tallying's choice). This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the participant's choice aligns with the TTB prediction. TTB will produce values close to 1.0, while Tallying will produce values close to 0.0, creating a massive and highly reliable gap between the two theories.

The chosen experimental design systematically pits Tallying against Take The Best. For 5 out of the 6 unique trials, the two heuristics make diametrically opposed predictions. This metric isolates those discriminating trials by filtering out any trials where Tallying predicts a tie, and computes the proportion of subject responses that align with the Tallying prediction. Data simulated under Tallying will yield values significantly above 0.5 (approaching 1.0 for low noise), whereas data simulated under TTB will yield values significantly below 0.5 (approaching 0.0), ensuring a massive contrast between the two theories with low between-subject variance.

This metric isolates trials where Tallying sees a strict tie (an equal number of feature wins for option A and option B). On these trials, Tallying is completely undiscriminating and predicts uniform guessing (50% accuracy). In contrast, WADD uses the validities (centered at chance) to break these ties, leading to a strong directional preference. By computing the proportion of times the subject's choice aligns with WADD's preference on these Tallying-tie trials, we expect a value near 0.5 for data generated by Tallying, and a value substantially above 0.5 for data generated by WADD.

By isolating specific trials where Tallying and the Weighted Additive Model (WADD) make opposite predictions, we can strongly separate the two theories. In Trial 3 and Trial 6, Tallying favors Option B because it wins on more features, whereas WADD strongly prefers Option A due to the high weight of the first feature. In Trial 5, Tallying prefers Option A for having more winning features, but WADD favors Option B. This metric calculates the average alignment with Tallying's predictions across these three highly discriminative trials. Tallying will yield values significantly above 0.5 (approaching 1.0), whereas WADD will yield values significantly below 0.5 (approaching 0.0).

This metric isolates trials 1, 3, and 4 from the experimental design. In these specific trials, the two options tie in the number of feature wins (Pure Tallying predicts a 50/50 guess), but one option strictly dominates the other in terms of feature validities regardless of the non-linear scaling parameter gamma. The Advocated Theory's tie-breaking mechanism therefore deterministically favors the validity-dominant option. By calculating the proportion of choices that align with the tie-breaker's prediction on these unambiguous trials, we expect the Advocated Theory to yield a value significantly above 0.5, while Pure Tallying will center tightly around 0.5.

This metric isolates trials where the two options are perfectly tied in the number of winning features (a tallying tie). According to the Advocated Theory (Pure Tallying), subjects have no basis for preference on these trials and must guess, resulting in a 50% alignment with any tie-breaking rule. The Competing Theory, however, postulates a validity-weighted tie-breaker when tallies are tied. The metric calculates the proportion of choices on tied trials that align with the higher validity-weighted option. The Competing Theory will predict a high alignment score (> 0.5), whereas Pure Tallying predicts exactly 0.5.

Pure Tallying relies exclusively on counting feature wins. On trials where the tally difference is exactly zero, Pure Tallying has no basis for preference and predicts a 50/50 guess, resulting in an expected absolute deviation from 0.5 near 0 (modulo binomial sampling noise). The Advocated theory, however, ALWAYS triggers its salience-weighted tie-breaker on these exact ties. Depending on the subject's 'gamma' parameter, the tie-breaker will consistently and strongly favor either the option with more valid features (if gamma > 0) or the option with less valid features (if gamma < 0). By computing the absolute deviation of the choice proportion from 0.5 on these 'exact tie' trials FOR EACH SUBJECT independently, we capture this systematic preference. Pure Tallying will yield a small value (binomial noise), whereas the Advocated theory will yield a large value (close to 0.5).

Pure Tallying treats exact ties in tally as a complete guess, predicting a 50/50 choice probability regardless of the features' validities. This means a subject's empirical choice proportion on exact tie trials will be close to 0.5, with small binomial variance. In contrast, the Competing Theory assumes that a tally difference of 0 always triggers a compensatory tie-breaker. Because the tie-breaker weights features by salience, it will strongly favor one option over the other (which one depends on the subject's gamma parameter). Consequently, the Competing Theory predicts deterministic or near-deterministic choices on these trials, leading to an empirical choice proportion far from 0.5. By computing the absolute deviation of each subject's choice proportion from 0.5 on exact tie trials, we expect a value near 0.1 for Pure Tallying and > 0.3 for the Competing Theory, highly discriminating the two.

This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject chooses the option that possesses the most valid feature (feature 1), conditional on only one option having it. The experimental design intentionally pits feature 1 against a larger number of less valid features. Pure Tallying ignores feature validities and strictly counts feature-wise wins, so it systematically chooses the option WITHOUT feature 1 in these trials (scoring near 0). The Advocated Theory (Additive Utility with power-law validities) heavily weights feature 1, causing subjects to systematically choose the option WITH feature 1 (scoring near 1). This provides a massive, stable contrast between the two models.

In Trials 1, 2, and 4, the Pure Tallying heuristic predicts either a preference for Option A (Trial 1) or a 50/50 guess (Trials 2 and 4), because Option A has either more feature-wise wins or an equal number of wins. By contrast, the Additive Utility (WADD) model strongly prefers Option B across all these trials because Option B dominates on the features with the highest objective validities. By calculating the proportion of times Option A is chosen across these specific trials, we expect Tallying to yield a value reliably >= 0.5, whereas WADD will yield a value significantly < 0.5.
